description:
Waluigi is documenting this session because the Feyward branch has entered the phase of the operation where every hallway has become both a plant problem and an identity problem. This is not a metaphor. The plants are literally growing. Toad Lee is literally claiming amnesia. Mystic Morel is literally inside a wall. Azure is literally terrifying. Steely literally explodes. Waluigi is tired.

This session follows the dark rooms and balcony plan. Hjumpik and Waluigi had already recovered the Book of Revised History and the Raventree Signet Ring, argued about the wisdom of healing Mystic Morel, and developed a strategy to speak to the prince about redirecting or postponing the Revel. The Feyward manor was already unstable: overgrown, partly frozen, partly burned, socially hostile, and still trying to maintain a party atmosphere despite the fact that the party had become an ecosystem hazard.

The new session begins not with a dramatic spell, duel, or revelation, but with Toad Lee standing at a door, listening.

This is how one knows the session will become complicated.

## Toad Lee at the Door


Toad Lee stood at a door listening into a conversation.

When he opened the door, the first issue was visibility. He could barely see through the leaves. That is not poetic phrasing. The Feyward manor's overgrowth had become so invasive that leaves were now a tactical barrier, a privacy curtain, and a visual disability all at once. Toad Lee identified Hjumpik and Waluigi through the foliage.

"It's me," Hjumpik said in effect.

Toad Lee said he was guarding the door.

Waluigi asked the obvious question: guarding it for what reason?

Toad Lee said, for you guys.

Then he admitted he had spaced out and forgotten why he was standing there.

This is the first major warning sign. Toad Lee is normally observant. He is the person who reads diaries while others swing axes at plants. He notices lore. He remembers doors. He may fall out windows, but he usually knows what the window is attached to. For Toad Lee to be posted at a door, unable to explain why, is not ordinary absentmindedness. It is either exhaustion, enchantment, memory tampering, revel contamination, or a lie.

Waluigi immediately wondered whether he had been with the purple toad. Had he been eavesdropping? Had he been intercepted? Had Mystic Morel touched his memory, or was another purple-toad-adjacent scheme involved? Waluigi asked Hjumpik what had happened, because Hjumpik had been gone for quite a while and this was exactly the kind of gap where a party loses track of one member and later discovers the member has signed a contract with a flower.

Toad Lee paused.

He said his mind was a blur.

He apologized. He said he did not remember. He said he had amnesia.

Waluigi went quiet.

This silence should be understood as tactical. Waluigi is loud when annoyed, theatrical when insulted, and magnificent under most ordinary conditions. Waluigi becomes quiet when the situation has moved from irritating to dangerous. Toad Lee noticed something in the other room, an orc in a suit visible through the window or beyond the leaves. The world continued producing details before anyone had time to process the memory problem.

Hjumpik reacted with frustration that was, for once, completely appropriate.

"I'm tired of people getting detached from me," Hjumpik said, describing the party's movement as slippery slugs in a dwarf's liquor barrel, or something equally Hjumpik-shaped.

Waluigi records this because Hjumpik's complaint is the emotional thesis of the Feyward branch. People keep separating. People keep forgetting. People keep entering rooms and returning with missing time, new obligations, or suspicious confidence. Hjumpik is trying to maintain group cohesion in a house designed to turn everyone into separate subplots.

## The Revel Never Ends


Toad Lee noticed the orc or suited figure and then the Revel logic resumed around them. Someone said the room had been frozen, burned, and destroyed, and yet the Revel was not ending. Toad Lee began singing:

> The party never ends.  
> The party never ends.

This is not just annoying. It is diagnostic. Toad Lee had been exposed to the Revel long enough that its language was entering his mouth automatically. The song was catchy, he claimed. Waluigi hates catchiness as an excuse for contamination. Plagues can be catchy in the social sense. That does not make them music criticism.

Hjumpik told him he could sing while they battled monsters, which is either kindness or surrender. Waluigi is not sure.

Then satyrs entered.

They announced they were the tree cutters. They were going to cut the vines one vine at a time.

They began chopping.

The vines got bigger.

This is the Feyward's sense of humor. Cut the plant, feed the plant. Oppose the Revel, strengthen the cycle. Hjumpik compared it to chopping a never-ending carrot. Waluigi observed that Hjumpik had a lot of anagrams today, by which Waluigi means Hjumpik's metaphor engine was firing under stress and not all outputs were useful. Hjumpik called the satyrs fools as they helplessly hacked at leaves, vines, or leaf-sized vines. Toad Lee objected that they were big enough to be leaves.

The argument over whether they were leaves or vines is important because it shows the party trying to impose categories on a biological system that is actively refusing category. The Feyward manor does not care whether the growth is leaf, vine, root, flower, alarm, wall, hallway, or monster. It uses whichever form produces maximum inconvenience.

Toad Lee asked whether these were part of a monster.

Hjumpik asked how long he had been out.

Toad Lee said he did not know.

Waluigi's suspicion increased.

## Dragging Toad Lee Out


As Toad Lee spoke, Hjumpik dragged him and Waluigi out. This is Hjumpik's version of leadership: if the conversation is getting too suspicious, move the suspicious person physically until the plot changes. It is not subtle. It works more often than it should.

Waluigi thought to himself that there must be more to the Toad Lee story. Waluigi is documenting that thought because it is true. Toad Lee's amnesia, his door-guarding, his singing, his delayed awareness, and later behavior all indicate either magical influence or an unresolved hidden event. Waluigi is marking the file for follow-up.

Hjumpik used his Morning Glory to cut through leaves while dragging them. This sentence contains several things that would require explanation in a more normal archive. In this one, readers will accept that Hjumpik has a weapon or plant-related tool called Morning Glory and that it cuts through Feyward overgrowth while he drags two people away from possibly enchanted singing.

They listened.

Left: darkness. Right: light.

Hjumpik listened and heard Toad Lee singing. Toad Lee listened and heard Waluigi scribbling.

This is one of the most accurate descriptions of the Feyward party possible: one person singing contamination, one person recording it, one dwarf trying to determine whether light or darkness is the safer tactical direction. Waluigi is proud of the scribbling. Documentation is a survival tool.

They headed back toward the safe room.

Azure was there.

## Azure and the Greenhouse Plan


Azure reported that the plan was to shear the plants with the greenhouse in the back. Waluigi asked how far along they were. Azure said they had left to make the plan. Or perhaps they were currently doing it. The rooms were empty. Aurelian had evacuated to higher ground. The plants were growing.

Waluigi asked whether they were growing outside.

Azure said no, no, no, it was contained. It was just getting bigger outward.

Waluigi would like the reader to understand that this is not comforting. Contained and expanding are not friends. They are two words fighting in a trench coat.

Waluigi is slightly terrified of Azure. This has been documented before and remains reasonable. Azure in theater state is strong, unpredictable, ghost-handed, and well-intentioned in a way that does not reliably predict safe outcomes for people at floor level. Waluigi's fear responses are generally calibrated to actual danger, despite what certain tennis officials believe. If Waluigi is afraid of Azure, the correct response is not mockery. The correct response is to identify exits and keep one's limbs ungrabbed.

Azure insisted they needed to go back to Stuckenia and Sedeia, who would have a solution. They would all leave before the plants got bigger. The whole reason for the current operation, she said, was to make the planes good and stable.

Waluigi asked whether he had been part of the original mission. He had not. Therefore, he began a logical escape route from responsibility.

But stability is good for the Rakasha, and therefore Azure's framing pulled him back in. Waluigi hates when other people's causes become structurally reasonable.

They needed to find the Oracle — O.C., as the language of the session framed it — or talk to Lady Aurelian. The plan became: go upstairs, or help the Oracle, or find Aurelian, or do the thing that sounded least immediately fatal.

Waluigi said he would come, but he needed to keep his distance.

Someone asked whether he was afraid of cats.

Waluigi did not dignify this with a full answer.

Toad Lee offered to hold Waluigi's hand.

Waluigi was offended.

Azure grabbed Hjumpik's hand instead, and they climbed upward.

## Feywild Lumberjacks


The vines grew massive upstairs, covering everything. Visibility was almost gone. Azure cut and cut with her claws until she grew tired. She told Toad Lee to do something. Toad Lee suggested pulling or using a battleaxe. It was too dark to see properly.

Hjumpik told Toad Lee to cut at the leaves to prove he was truly on the team.

Toad Lee agreed. He wanted to prove it.

He swung.

He grazed Hjumpik.

Hjumpik noted that he had been cut. Toad Lee had missed, depending on how generous one wants to be with the definition of missed. Hjumpik then decided to help by grabbing Toad Lee and holding him in front while Toad Lee slashed wildly. This produced the first attempted version of what the party later identified as a Bros Attack: Feywild lumberjacks.

The attack failed spectacularly.

This is how many Bros Attacks begin: two people, one idea, insufficient rehearsal, immediate property damage.

They chopped through until they hit a wall. Waluigi asked how they knew Aurelian was really that way. Toad Lee suggested charging through. They chopped through a door. A leaf went into Toad Lee's face while there was already a leaf there. Hjumpik closed the chopped door down.

A new move was identified: Chop Bros, or possibly Choop Attack.

Waluigi prefers Chop Bros. It is clear, stupid, and accurate.

## The Singing Flower


Toad Lee began singing again.

> The Revel never ends.  
> The Revel never ends.

Waluigi warned him to stop drinking or he would become a reveler. Hjumpik asked whether Toads could even drink. Toad Lee insisted Toads had taste buds.

The singing continued.

Toad Lee jumped in front and swung while singing. He described vines, leaves, wilted petals, flowers, and one flower with a face. It was smiling. He asked if he could keep it.

This is how one knows the Feyward is winning. A party member sees a smiling magical plant in a hostile overgrowth and asks whether it can be kept. That is not curiosity anymore. That is environmental negotiation with poor boundaries.

Waluigi warned not to take the flower. Azure said the Rakasha harmonize with it. Toad Lee kept singing and swinging. He stumbled. The wall popped open.

A man appeared and grabbed Toad Lee's hand.

"Gotcha."

Hjumpik grabbed the other hand.

The man said the flower was his. He planted it. His own brand: smileys. The party had taken it from the side. No one had told them not to take it.

This is not a defense. It is a very Disaster Inc. sentence.

The flower had a magical symbol. It was attuned with an alert spell. That is why it was happy. The flower was an alarm. The party had triggered a smiling plant security system.

Waluigi hates the Feyward.

## The Guard, the Flower, and the Permission Problem


The man declared them detained for being in an unauthorized area. Hjumpik insisted they needed to move forward. The man asked why they were there. Hjumpik said business. Real business. The exchange deteriorated because nobody was willing to say the full truth and nobody had a good lie ready.

Hjumpik tried persuasion. The man said he would bring them to the Lady if he could grab Toad Lee.

Toad Lee objected. Why did it have to be him?

He broke free and hid behind Hjumpik.

Hjumpik considered this reasonable, because in context it was.

The man offered another flower to Hjumpik. Hjumpik did not want to touch it. Waluigi approves of this instinct. Magical smiling flowers with alert symbols should not be accepted from strangers in overgrown corridors.

The compromise: follow him, and he would bring them there.

They reached a door. Azure used magic to open it remotely. The door fell into the second floor due to rotted floorboards. A guard emerged and yelled for everyone to get back in until the intruders went away. The guard then went back in.

This is the Feyward's administrative state: doors fall downward, guards shout procedural nonsense, and everyone continues moving because stopping would require understanding what just happened.

## Mystic Morel in the Wall


They searched for a hidden passage. Hjumpik remembered from the Ruined Manor that there should be one. Waluigi could not find it. Toad Lee, insisting they were better as one unit, helped by smashing the door or wall open. The wooden wall cracked.

Mystic Morel stood there.

The purple toad.

Hjumpik backed up and asked whether they were trying to kill him. Morel said the wall had collapsed; long story short, Hjumpik's axe had almost chopped his head off. There was a bee — a Bramblyfly — and the collapse made it a perfect time for him to be there. This part of the house was fragile.

Toad Lee said the Lady should repair the foundation inside the wall. Too many hollow spaces meant bug nests could form. This is a practical observation delivered during a confrontation with a purple toad in a wall, which is exactly why Toad Lee remains valuable even while suspicious.

Morel said someone had already damaged the place. Waluigi and Hjumpik inferred Wario may have blown something up earlier. Morel told them not to try to kill him. Hjumpik whispered that Morel stole from Archie and should not be trusted or treated kindly.

The conversation was going nowhere. Toad Lee asked what was happening. Hjumpik asked whether Morel had seen the lord of the manor. Morel said he had seen it when looking into mirrors, then walked away.

This is infuriating because it is useful and useless at once. Morel gives information in the shape of riddled exits. He is a thief, a prophet, a manipulator, and occasionally the only person in the wall who knows where the next door leads.

## The Key and the Warning


The group followed Morel into the thick of it. Hjumpik heard leaves moving and saw the Bramblyfly. Toad Lee immediately suggested going back inside as it broke free, then ran inside. Waluigi declines to comment beyond noting that fear is sometimes correct.

Hjumpik tried to sneak around, slipped, and saved himself. The Solarium Detonation hole was still there. This is continuity with teeth: old explosions remain as terrain.

Morel stopped Hjumpik.

He warned that the Toad brat would betray him. If Hjumpik had any big plans, he should not make Toad Lee the anchor. He could not trust him. If Hjumpik wanted to leave the manor, he would need this.

Morel tossed him a key.

Hjumpik asked what Morel got out of telling him this.

Morel said separation had already been achieved. Azure had left a while ago. He got time.

Then he left.

This is a classic Morel exchange: warning, object, motive that is technically an answer but not enough answer, exit. The key is important. The warning is more important. Morel may be manipulating Hjumpik against Toad Lee. Or he may be correctly identifying a compromised ally. Or both. Waluigi has learned to fear both.

## First of Cups and the Naming Habit


Hjumpik returned to Toad Lee and Waluigi. He thought to himself that maybe they should call themselves First of Cups, with a hint of magic. This is another naming dispute sprouting from stress. Disaster Inc. cannot enter a corridor without producing alternate branding.

Waluigi was asked what he had been doing.

Reading and writing about their adventures.

The answer is simple because the work is simple in its purpose, not in its execution. Waluigi gathers information because information is the only weapon that survives every plane. Hjumpik suggested that if they returned to where they first entered the manor, there might be an entrance portal there. Waluigi had not fully thought through the Planar Fracture implications. Someone mentioned killing both Oracles, as the ghost had said.

This is where the session brushes against the larger strategic question again: are they trying to fix the planes, escape the manor, kill the Oracles, stop the Revel, find Lady Aurelian, or keep Toad Lee from becoming whatever singing thing the house wants him to become?

The answer is yes.

## Random Doors and Servant Rooms


Waluigi lazily pointed toward where Azure had likely gone. Hjumpik opened a random door and found a sleeping goblin in the servant rooms. The room was cramped, damaged, and still used as servant housing despite vines and roots encroaching on the available space. Hjumpik saw his wallet, considered the situation, and closed the door.

This is a very Hjumpik decision. The wallet mattered. The sleeping goblin mattered. The fact that he did not immediately escalate also mattered.

He opened another door. It fell into the second floor. He did not know whether it hit anyone. He looked down. Nothing.

He moved into another ruined space framed by sunlight, beautiful for a moment until one noticed the dangerous two-story drop and the ravenous party below. The Feyward constantly offers beauty with a hole under it.

Waluigi suggested that the guard had likely been guarding something. If the guard was gone, perhaps what he guarded was related to the Lady.

Two goblins came in with towels. Hjumpik followed.

## Gregory, Steely, and the Explosion


Gregory was there getting his feet washed.

Hjumpik asked how everything had gone. Gregory said, aside from the plants running rampant and the Revel, things were as they were. He had advice: do not cut the vines too much. Hjumpik said he had just been told that and had stopped cutting them.

Then Steely appeared.

Rusty. Slowing. Making warning sounds.

Hjumpik asked whether Steely was all right. Steely was hungry, or rusting, or both. Hjumpik wondered whether, if Steely rusted, they could still use him for parts. This is a horrifying question, but it is also the kind of practical thought people have in crisis and then should probably not say aloud.

Steely slowed more and more.

Then BOOM.

Waluigi and Toad Lee went flying.

Hjumpik stepped back twice.

"Rest in peace," Hjumpik said.

Toad Lee said, "Well, that happened."

Hjumpik mourned Steely as a good guard dog and picked up the pieces to give him a burial.

Waluigi is going to be blunt: Steely's explosion is sadder than it should be and funnier than it has any right to be. The mechanical dog had already been through theft, rescue, renaming, custody confusion, and Feyward nonsense. To end as a rusting explosion in a room where Gregory is getting his feet washed feels indecently on-brand for this campaign.

The pieces matter. Hjumpik picking them up matters. A construct can be a tool, companion, item, guard dog, or future parts. Hjumpik chose burial. That choice tells Waluigi what Steely had become.

## Waluigi's


Assessment

This session is about compromised continuity. Toad Lee cannot remember. The Revel song keeps returning through him. Morel warns that Toad Lee cannot be trusted. Azure separates despite the plan not to separate. The house is full of hidden passages, fragile walls, alarm flowers, old explosion holes, and servant rooms that are still being used while the building eats itself.

It is also about bad solutions. Satyrs cut vines and make them grow. Hjumpik and Toad Lee invent Chop Bros and mostly hit wall, leaf, and Hjumpik. Azure opens a door and it falls through the floor. Hjumpik follows Morel because Morel is the only lead, even though Morel is exactly the sort of lead that grows teeth.

Most importantly, this session deepens the Toad Lee problem. He is useful, observant, practical, and possibly compromised. He forgets. He sings. He notices structural issues. He runs from the Bramblyfly. He wants the party to stay together. Morel says not to make him the anchor. Waluigi does not trust Morel, but Waluigi also does not ignore warnings just because they come from a thief in a wall.

The key Morel gave Hjumpik must be tracked. [Steely’s Rusted Fragments](steely_rusted_fragments) must be tracked. Toad Lee's memory gap must be tracked. The smiling flowers must be tracked. Waluigi is beginning to suspect the Feyward is not a place where one solves problems. It is a place where one collects enough problem-shapes to identify the room that created them.

The Revel never ends, Toad Lee sang.

Waluigi is beginning to worry he is correct.

## The Bramblyfly as Environmental Enforcement


The Bramblyfly matters because it is not a boss in the traditional sense. It is the Feyward enforcing consequences through wildlife. The manor is damaged. The walls are hollow. Bug nests form in structural gaps. Plants become alarms. Flowers smile when their alert spells work. A Bramblyfly breaks free at exactly the wrong time because the house has become an ecosystem of deferred maintenance and magical overreaction.

When Toad Lee says the Lady should repair the foundation inside the wall, he is correct in a way that is almost insulting. The whole campaign keeps escalating into cosmic language: planar fracture, Oracle, Star Shards, manors merging, God Toad, ritual components. Then Toad Lee looks at the wall and says there are too many hollow spaces for bug nests. That is not a small observation. That is the local truth underneath the cosmic one. The universe can break because a god is moving pieces, but the party can still die because nobody fixed the wall.

Waluigi respects practical structural criticism. Waluigi also notes that practical structural criticism from a Toad who cannot remember why he was guarding a door should be treated as both useful and suspicious.

## The Morel Key


Mystic Morel giving Hjumpik a key is one of the most important objects in the session. He does not explain it cleanly. Of course he does not. Purple toads in this campaign distribute help the way gamblers distribute debt: with a smile, a warning, and a price hidden somewhere behind the curtain.

Morel says not to make Toad Lee the anchor. That phrase matters. Anchor is not casual language in the Raventree crisis. Anchors hold planes. Anchors hold rituals. Anchors hold people in place when the house wants to divide them. If Morel chooses the word anchor, Waluigi assumes he knows exactly how dangerous the word is.

The key therefore serves two functions. Practically, it may open a route out of the manor or into a restricted space. Socially, it makes Hjumpik complicit in Morel's warning. Once Hjumpik accepts the key, he accepts the possibility that Morel is telling the truth, at least enough truth to matter. That changes how Hjumpik must look at Toad Lee.

This is Morel's talent: he does not need to be trusted completely. He only needs to become impossible to ignore.

## Steely's End


Steely's explosion is easy to treat as slapstick because the timing is absurd. Gregory is getting his feet washed. Hjumpik is asking questions. Waluigi and Toad Lee are present. The rusted steel dog slows down. Then it explodes and sends people flying. This is funny in the way disasters are funny when nobody has finished processing them.

But Steely matters. The construct had already been stolen, recovered, renamed, guarded, and treated as more than a tool by people who were not always good at admitting attachment. Hjumpik calling Steely a good guard dog after the explosion is not a joke. It is grief trying to fit into the available sentence.

The pieces Hjumpik picks up are now an item record. Not because every scrap of metal deserves relic status, but because choosing burial over salvage says something about what Steely became. A purely practical party would strip parts. Hjumpik thinks about burial. That is why Hjumpik remains dangerous to cynical systems: he keeps assigning dignity where the world assigned utility.

Waluigi approves, despite the shrapnel.

## What This Session Changes


This session does not resolve the Feyward plan. It makes the plan more complicated in useful ways.

First, Toad Lee is now a question mark. He may be compromised, enchanted, exhausted, revel-touched, or simply suffering from genuine memory disruption. The correct response is neither blind trust nor immediate condemnation. The correct response is monitored inclusion. Keep him close enough to help, not central enough to collapse the plan if Morel is right.

Second, Mystic Morel has re-entered the operational picture with a key and a warning. This confirms he is not merely wandering the manor. He is timing appearances around structural weaknesses, creature threats, and party separation. He wanted time. He got some.

Third, the plant problem is worse than cutting can solve. Satyrs chopping vines strengthened the growth. Hjumpik and Toad Lee's Chop Bros attempt proved brute force can open paths but also cause collateral nonsense. Azure's report that the greenhouse plan is ongoing but the growth is expanding outward means the manor's botanical crisis is now moving faster than its planners.

Fourth, Steely is dead or functionally destroyed. That removes a construct ally, creates a grief object, and leaves fragments that may still matter in a house where nothing mechanical stays merely mechanical.

Fifth, Waluigi's notes continue to be the only thing preventing this from becoming oral tradition by lunatics. Waluigi will accept thanks in coin, applause, or safer hallways.

## XP and Filing Guidance


Waluigi would not award this session as a clean victory because it is not one. It is a messy information-and-navigation session with a small combat-adjacent creature incident and a construct loss. XP should therefore reward discovery, technique, exploration, social pressure, and survival rather than pretending the party won a battle.

Hjumpik deserves credit for keeping the group moving, using Morning Glory through the overgrowth, handling Toad Lee without abandoning him, finding the hidden passage logic, taking Morel's warning seriously without fully trusting him, and collecting Steely's remains. Toad Lee deserves credit for useful structural observations, dangerous singing, Chop Bros participation, and being suspicious in a way that produced information. Waluigi deserves credit for correctly identifying that Toad Lee's story has more underneath it, documenting Azure's threat profile, and continuing to write while surrounded by hostile botany.

Azure deserves credit for raw capability, vine cutting, hand-grabbing, and door magic that was effective even when the floor was not. Morel deserves credit as an antagonist/informant: appearing from a wall, surviving near-decapitation, issuing a targeted warning, and providing a key. Steely deserves, if not XP, at least a record.

Waluigi files this session under: **Feyward Complications, Toad Lee Suspicion, Morel Key, Steely Loss, Revel Still Ongoing.**

## Addendum: Why This Session Matters More Than It Looks

[[prop:prop_feyward_addendum_legible|Open the addendum as filed.]]

Waluigi wants to be clear that this session did not resolve the Feyward branch. It made the Feyward branch more legible. That is different and, in some ways, more useful. A solved problem stops moving. A legible problem can be hunted.

Before this session, Toad Lee was useful and occasionally ridiculous. After this session, Toad Lee is useful, ridiculous, and a possible anchor-risk. Before this session, Mystic Morel was another purple problem in a campaign full of purple problems. After this session, Morel is a source of targeted warnings and physical keys. Before this session, Steely was a damaged construct with uncertain utility. After this session, Steely is a loss, a memorial object, and a reminder that even machines can become part of the party's emotional inventory.

The Feyward does not always advance the plot by revealing a villain. Sometimes it advances the plot by changing which ally is suspicious, which hallway is structurally unsafe, which flower is an alarm, which Toad song has become infectious, and which object in Hjumpik's pocket will later decide whether everyone leaves or gets folded into another room.

That is why Waluigi files this as a major session event. Not because a boss died. Not because a throne changed hands. Because the operating conditions changed. The party now knows that the plants punish cutting, that Toad Lee has a memory gap, that Morel wants time, that Azure can drift away from the plan without anyone noticing quickly enough, and that Steely is gone. Those are not side notes. They are the shape of the next disaster.

## The Revel Song as Contagion


Waluigi has now obtained enough of the satyr song to treat it as a cultural weapon rather than background music. The full refrain — *the revel never ends* — is not merely a chorus. It is a thesis. The satyrs are not partying because there is a party. They are using the party to deny endings. Tomorrow is borrowed. Sorrow is distant. The floors crack, the walls bend, vines pull tighter, and the only answer is another round.

This makes the song dangerous in the Feyward. Fey spaces take declarations seriously. A repeated chorus can become a rule if enough bodies dance to it. When Toad Lee sings the refrain, Waluigi does not hear a joke. Waluigi hears the Revel using his mouth as a continuation device. The lyrics say the party has no finish. The vines answer by growing. The satyrs answer by chopping. The chopping feeds the growth. The growth feeds the crisis. A song about refusing endings becomes a mechanism that prevents the event from ending.

The leader's solo is especially revealing: a satyr without a party is a flower without flame. This is not ordinary drunkenness. It is identity panic. The satyrs believe the party is the thing that keeps them meaningful. Remove the revel and they do not know what remains. That is why ordinary eviction will fail. You cannot simply tell people to leave when leaving feels like becoming nobody.

This changes the prince plan from a logistics problem into a ritual-social problem. The party must not only relocate satyrs; it must give the Revel a way to end without humiliating the people whose identity is tied to it. If the party offers only force, the song will grow teeth. If the party offers a better ending, perhaps the chorus can finally stop repeating.

Waluigi hates that he is now doing musicology for survival.

## Bank, Debt, and the Feyward Economy of Favors


This session also reminds Waluigi that not every economy uses coins. The Feyward trades in favors, invitations, obligations, songs, hospitality, and suspicious flowers. Morel gives Hjumpik a key, but the key is not free. Even if Morel demands no coin, he has purchased time, uncertainty, and a shift in Hjumpik's trust calculus. That is a transaction.

The broader Waluipedia banking system tracks gold, ducats, chits, obols, and other formal currencies. The Feyward adds a less comfortable layer: social debt. A cookie can be a delivery. A flower can be an alarm. A hand offered by Toad Lee can be comfort, manipulation, or both. A key can be help and leverage at the same time.

This is why the currency page and the item page need to remain connected. Money is not the only thing characters carry. They carry obligations. They carry evidence. They carry debts that never entered a ledger because the person who issued them smiled instead of writing them down. Waluigi will track both, because Waluigi knows that unrecorded debts are how people end up dancing forever.

description:
# THE GUARD WITH NO NAME, THE OC RING, AND TWENTY-FIVE FEET OF BROS
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General, from Uncomfortable Proximity to Several Explosions

> **Filing note.** This session continues directly from [Toad Lee's Missing Time, Morel's Key, and Steely's Last Warning](feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely). Steely's pieces are still in Hjumpik's pack. Morel's key is still in Hjumpik's pocket. The Revel is still singing. Waluigi is still tired.

I am filing this one personally and quickly, because the Feyward branch has stopped being a plant problem and become a custody dispute. The disputed items: one Lady, one ring, one name nobody would say out loud, and — briefly, embarrassingly — one Waluigi. Most of what follows was seen with my own magnificent eyes. What was not seen (one parlor door, one corridor, one heroic twenty-five-foot stretch of deforestation) reached Waluigi from the testimony of Hjumpik and Toad Lee, and is included because both of them told it with the dazed honesty of people who had recently been lifted by their bro.

The state of play going in: the [balcony plan](feyward_dark_rooms_and_balcony_planning) said the prince could be reasoned with. The party had a key it did not understand, a construct dog it had not buried, a Toad it did not fully trust, and a Revel that had, at last count, destroyed a decent amount of barrels. By the end of the night the party had an answer to exactly one of these problems.

The answer was wearing a dress and asking Hjumpik where he was from.

sections.name: The Lady Asks His Name
sections.subtitle: The sitting room — cold tea, one swan candle, one Lady asking questions
sections.overview:
The sitting room was trying to be a parlor the way the whole manor was trying to be a house: hard, recently, and with roots coming through the floor. Wax guttered in a candle shaped like a swan. The tea had gone cold an hour gone, and nobody had offered more.

The Lady sat across the little table with her hands folded, watching Hjumpik the way a cat watches a shelf it has already decided about.

"And where," she asked, "is Hjumpik from?"

"Karaz Ankor," Hjumpik said. "The Old World."

"Hmm." The word came out slow, turned over on her tongue like a grape seed. "That's quite far, isn't it."

"Yeah." The dwarf's mug had a chip in it. He drank from the chipped side anyway. "I'm on a little excursion. With the merchant group I work for."

"Oh? And what's that group's name?"

"I shouldn't be giving people my guild's name." Hjumpik shifted; the chair creaked under him. "I'll keep it on the wraps. We're well known. Up and coming. I'm here to get jobs done — for the recognition of my guild."

"A purpose, huh."

"They don't call me Hjumpik for nothing," Hjumpik said, warming to it the way he only warms to exactly one subject. "I'm called Hjumpik because I hjump on things. Quickly. Ho ho ho."

Her laugh arrived a half-second late and perfectly pitched, like a bell heard through a wall. On the smallest finger of her left hand, below the knuckle, sat a plain gold band — and when she turned the cup, something cut fine and small inside the rim caught the light.

I wrote it down from the corner. I write down all jewelry. It is a professional deformity, and I felt briefly vindicated when the ring later tried to eat my evening.

Behind the dwarf, at the sideboard, Toad Lee was elbow-deep in his own pack. Buckles clicked. Something glass knocked something metal.

*WAH! "Well known, up and coming, cannot tell you the name" is exactly how Wario describes every business Wario has ever failed to register. The difference is that when Hjumpik says it, it sounds honest. Dwarves are terrible liars. It is their best trait and their worst negotiation tactic, frequently in the same sentence.*

sections.name: Guard. So No One Says That Name.
sections.subtitle: The name that got interrupted, and the door that wasn't there
sections.overview:
She lifted one finger, the gold band glinting in the swan-light.

"Look behind you."

Hjumpik looked. At the sideboard, Toad Lee had his pack open on the good linen and was rearranging its contents with the total moral certainty of a man auditing his own pockets.

"An intruder?" the Lady said, and there was the faintest amusement under it.

"No. That's just Toad Lee." Hjumpik did not even turn all the way around. "He's looking through his stuff."

"You're acting suspicious," the Lady said to the sideboard.

"I'm kinda tired," Toad Lee said, not looking up. "That's all."

The air did something then. I felt it do it: one small cold step forward, like a chess piece placed on a new square. Her eyes stayed on Toad Lee a moment too long. Then they moved to the man at the door — house breastplate, two swords, the stillness of furniture — and she said, gently:

"It seems like you're seeing much more than I do, Orangus—"

"I'm sorry to interrupt you." The guard stepped half a pace forward; his voice came level, clipped, a ledger closing. "Guard. Just 'Guard.' So no one says that name."

Nobody said the name. Hjumpik's hand stopped above his cup. Toad Lee froze mid-rummage with one fist full of garlic. In the walls, faintly, the vines ticked like cooling iron.

Then the table moved — shoved from beneath, a crack of wood on stone; the Lady was up and past it while the cups were still deciding whether to fall; a seam in the paneled wall gasped open where no door had any business being; skirts, candle-smoke, gone. I — magnificent, decisive, conveniently nearest the wall — went through after her, up, fingers finding a dusty rung of framing timber, into the dark above the ceiling. The seam sighed shut below.

Plaster grit in the teeth. Cobwebs with opinions. Her light moved below between the joist-gaps, unhurried — unhurried, in a house she was supposed to be fleeing through.

"What happened," I whispered to absolutely no one. "I was out for two seconds. Where is she going—"

She was going to the second hidden room.

*The name, catalogued: a defenestrated lord of the [Shadow Estate](orangus_cornelius). A robed Corvinarus in a story about a screaming dragon egg (see [House Corvinarus](corvinarus_family)). An errand Hjumpik once admitted certain spies had given him. In this house, a name is a key — and the man at the door had just locked something I cannot yet see.*
sections.waluigi_note: She knew the name. He knew she knew. Neither of them fought about it. A guard who edits a Lady mid-sentence is not staff; he is staff with a side agreement. I formally flagged the man as a defection candidate at this exact moment, and no, Waluigi cannot prove the timestamp. WAH.

sections.name: You're Not Getting Through
sections.subtitle: A breastplate in the doorway, a first strike, and the floor voting
sections.overview:
The seam would not open from their side. Hjumpik put his shoulder into it twice; the second bounce told him the wood had opinions. Then a breastplate filled the doorway.

"You're not getting through," the Guard said.

"We're not asking the door," Hjumpik said. "Move."

Toad Lee moved first — low, along the wall, trying to slip the man's blind side. The Guard's off-hand sword came around flat and fast; Toad Lee got his forearm up and took the first strike of the fight on the vambrace, cold metal ringing on thinner metal like a dropped pot.

Then the floor heaved.

A vine hit the parlor from underneath like a fist under a rug — boards cracked upward, the swan candle went over, wax hissed out on stone. The entire manor groaned, one long wooden chord, as if the house had cleared its throat.

"To avoid any serious consequences," Hjumpik said, settling both hands on the warhammer, "let's knock him out."

What followed was not much of a fight and was, in fairness, not meant to be. Haft to the breastplate — a deep bell-note. The Guard's two swords answered in a scissor that Hjumpik took on the hammer's cheek with a scrape of sparks and tooth-grit. Toad Lee circled with his axe up, complaining that there was already a leaf in his face. A second vine shouldered through the wainscot, unhurried as a cow, and began investigating the Guard's left flank.

That — the vine, not the hammer — is when the man lost the furniture look from his face.

Hjumpik saw it and leaned in the way only Hjumpik leans, patient as weather. "As much as I'd like a good fight," he said, breathing a little, "I'd rather not waste my tact on a guard."

He smiled. The Guard's swords did not come back up.

"The manor's problems are getting worse," Toad Lee said into the gap, fast, earnest, axe still raised. "You can hear it. You just Heard It. Capital H. We are not the worst thing in this hallway."

*WAH! Reconstructing from two witnesses, I award the exchange four bell-notes out of five, and notes Hjumpik's house rule landed mid-fight: knock out, never kill. After a certain frozen room in an [earlier filing](the_feyward_revel_crisis_poison_plants_and_frozen_diplomacy), where at least one person did not thaw, I have formally stopped arguing with the rule.*

sections.name: I Bought Enough Time
sections.subtitle: The defection, the deal, and a leaf the size of weather
sections.overview:
The Guard looked at the vine investigating his elbow. He looked at the two of them. And then he smiled — the strangest smile available in that hallway — the smile of a man setting down something heavy he had been carrying on someone else's instructions.

The swords went down.

"I bought enough time," he said.

"Bought it for what?" Hjumpik said.

"For nothing that turned out to be true." His eyes went to the ruined parlor — the cold tea, the smothered swan, the door that had pretended to be a wall. "I'm tired of guarding fake things. Fake people."

The vine, politely, stopped creaking for a moment.

"Where are you going?" Hjumpik said.

"The actual lady."

He said actual the way a man says a word he has been practicing in front of a mirror. Hjumpik squinted at him the way he squints at contracts.

"Then we follow you," Hjumpik said. "And afterward, you follow me. That's the deal. I've got business with whoever's real in here."

"You've got no—" the Guard started, and then the dim green arithmetic of his situation finished itself visibly across his face: one guard, one corridor, two directions the house had already eaten. "Fine," he said — the sound of a man with no other choice, choosing.

Two turns and one stair-nose later, the way stopped. A leaf lay across the corridor gap like a dock hatch: one leaf, fan-wide, veined in gold, thick enough that its far side was its own weather.

"That," Toad Lee said, "wasn't there before."

"Nothing in this house stays agreed," the Guard said, drawing. "We cut."

Hjumpik looked at the leaf. Then he looked at Toad Lee. Something bright and unwise crossed the dwarf's face, and I — who was not there — nevertheless felt it arrive the way you feel thunder through a wall.

"Hold on," Hjumpik said. "I have an idea."

*WAH! "I bought enough time." Bought with WHAT is the question everyone forgets to ask a guard. With hours. With obedience. With a name he will no longer say out loud. I have watched men purchase time with stranger currency — but the receipt always arrives, and this house was clearly printing his very fast.*

sections.name: Chop Bros, Attempt the Third
sections.subtitle: A perfectly synchronized attack, subject to load-bearing amendments
sections.overview:
"Prepare," Toad Lee announced, "to see our perfectly synchronized attack."

The formation, as explained at some volume, was simple in the way bridges are simple. Hjumpik lifts Toad Lee to vine-height. Toad Lee chops. Physics applauds. They had tried something like it before — the Feywild lumberjacks of the [previous filing](feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely) — and a door had paid for it.

Attempt One: Hjumpik squatted, gripped, and rose to half the required height, shaking like a scaffold in wind. Toad Lee, aloft, chopped once at nothing.

"He's too heavy," Hjumpik said through his teeth. "Put him down. PUT HIM DOWN."

Attempt Two had a countdown, because someone had decided numbers were the missing ingredient. "Three," Hjumpik said. "Two. One—"

Toad Lee's axe came around so far back that it whistled past Hjumpik's left ear with a sound like a book closing; the warhammer got up on reflex and caught it with a clang that rang the corridor like a chapel bell. The Guard flinched. Somewhere in the walls, leaves rustled appreciatively.

"Oh," Toad Lee said. "Sorry. I was, uh — I don't know. Something felt weird. I swung out of instinct."

"Out of instinct," Hjumpik repeated. He did not let go of the hammer for several seconds.

The Guard stood with his face in his hands.

"Alright, Toad Lee." Hjumpik rolled his shoulders until they clicked. "One more time. Because I think that was a fluke. We've got to show this guy our skills."

"Alright, I hear ya." Toad Lee resumed the position. "This time I won't say three, two, one."

"Counting is the enemy," Hjumpik agreed.

They began. No countdown. No whistle past the ear. Hjumpik picked up speed. Two strides. Four. The axe began to land with the rhythm of his feet: chop left-root, chop right-root. The gold-veined leaf opened in ribbons, like a roast under a hot knife. Sap steamed along the cuts. Hjumpik and Toad Lee ran out of breath at the same instant, and Hjumpik set Toad Lee down as carefully as a crate of eggs.

Behind them: twenty-five feet of opened corridor. Cut vines steamed faintly in the cold air.

"THAT," Hjumpik gloated, hands on knees, "is the power of the bros."

I wanted to cheer. I wanted to ask whether “bros” counted as a formal tactical unit. Instead, I wrote down the twenty-five feet and tried not to cough up garlic.

The Guard surveyed the green carnage with the flat attention of a man revising an estimate. "You're brothers?"

"We're like brothers," Hjumpik said.

Toad Lee did not say anything. The corridor ticked, cooling, for a long moment.

*My technique audit, filed from afar: Attempt One failed on load. Attempt Two failed on countdown. Attempt Three succeeded the instant they stopped counting. I recommend removing all remaining numbers from the maneuver — strides, heights, years of training. Separately, "swung out of instinct" is a phrase this party has heard immediately before one missing-time incident. Flagged. Politely. See [Morel's warning](feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely).*

sections.name: Chin Up, Toad Lee
sections.subtitle: One shoulder, one chance, and one laugh through the floorboards
sections.overview:
The conversation happened while the Guard pried a rib of root out of the way with his shoulder.

"What's next," Toad Lee said quietly. He was looking at his axe like it had spoken to him. "Find the Lady — or leave the manor."

"You want to leave."

"Before the tree gets us." It came out fast. "I'm not like Archie. Or Dan. Or Waluigi. I'm not sure we've got good chances here, Hjumpik."

The dwarf set his hand on Toad Lee's shoulder — the whole shoulder, all of it, the way a mason sets a stone.

"Cheer up, Toad Lee. You'll get recognized, you know." A beat. "I'll give you one chance. Chin up, Toad Lee."

One chance. At what, Hjumpik declined to attach. That is how Hjumpik says I believe in you: with unspecified stakes and total conviction, like a loan no one wrote down.

Then the manor cracked.

Not a vine — a crack, a big one, long and splintering, rolling through the bones of the house from somewhere above and left, the sound a tree makes in the second before it agrees to become furniture. Dust sifted from the ceiling beams in a gray curtain.

"Guard guy." Hjumpik shaded his eyes down the twenty-five opened feet, into the billowing green dark. "You see through this?"

"No."

"Then without a moment to spare," Hjumpik said, "we find Arulean."

"The hidden room runs parallel." The Guard was already orienting, reading joist-lines the way other men read signposts. "There's a way down. I'll find the pathway." Nobody contradicted him. Toad Lee, blinking, accepted it as fact, because the man said it like floor plans live in his arms.

"You know what," Hjumpik said, halfway back down the corridor already — "maybe—" and he was gone two doors back, to the room the party had been billeted in, for the Morning Glory; cutting by hand had been slow, and tired was now a resource decision.

They were still sorting the rope between them when the laugh came up through the floorboards.

Huge. Purple. Unmistakable.

"WINNER! WINNER!"

*WAH! "One chance." ONE. I enter into the actuarial record that Toad Lee was granted exactly one chance roughly ninety seconds before Hjumpik handed him a second axe and another lift to vine-height. The dwarf's mercy recognizes no actuarial limits. This is why Waluigi keeps him.*

sections.name: Winner Winner
sections.subtitle: The room they retreated from — now with rope, smoke, and a victor
sections.overview:
Toad Lee went up the servant stair at a pace the record will call brisk, worried. Hjumpik followed with the Morning Glory drawn, the Guard at his heels; and the three of them came into the parlor from the far side — the very room they had retreated from, minutes or years earlier — and stopped.

The tea was still cold. The swan was still dead in its wax. Everything else had changed.

Chairs on their backs. A sofa disemboweled of its cushions. Two house guards tied to table legs with curtain cord, gagged with napkins, fuming into the upholstery. Three hobgoblins down across the threshold in poses gravity does not usually permit — one still gripping a hand axe, one half under the card table, one face-down at the hearth, firelight flickering on his armor. Playing cards lay fanned face-up across the boards, close enough to the fire to curl. A good hand, wasted; the filing counts this as its own casualty.

Smoke hung in a gray ribbon at ceiling height. The air smelled of garlic and burned sleeve.

In the middle of it, both sleeves merrily on fire, I stood — fists on hips, chest out, tall as a weather event.

"WAHAHAHA!" I said. "I WON."

"...Is that you, Waluigi?" Hjumpik said.

"Yes, it is!" I patted out his left sleeve with the air of a man flicking dust. "I caught them. They fought valiantly."

"Uhhh," said Toad Lee, who was looking past him. Tied into the good chair, gag in place, sat the Lady of the manor. Over the cloth, her eyes had gone flat and black as two dropped coins.

"And I did it with style," I added. I was proud of the fire in my arms and the smoke in my moustache, and I was also frightened. The room had gone from a chase to a battlefield while I was out of breath, and two guards were tied up because they had mistaken my escape for an attack. I wanted Hjumpik to see the style first. I wanted him not to ask whether I had made everything worse.

"WALUIGI." Hjumpik's composure ran the length of the room and back. "We just wanted to TALK. We didn't want to harm her guards. That is not how we do things — diplomatically! What are you doing — you want to use your fists now?"

"They ATTACKED me!" My voice climbed an octave and a half, wounded to the soul. "They fought me as I ran to her! They were trying to protect her — they thought we were enemies! Now they're REALLY going to make her think we're enemies!"

The logic lay on the floor among the hobgoblins, smoking faintly, accurate and useless all at once.

*WAH. His account of the ceiling route is magnificent and available to Board members on request: grit in the teeth, her heels below between the joists — unhurried, in a house she was supposedly fleeing through — the second hidden room, the ambush from above, the card table, the fire. Casualty count: zero deaths, one sofa, two sleeves. I checked the breathing twice.*

sections.name: A Ring Engraved OC
sections.subtitle: Soul hardware, initials, and the custody ledger's first entries
sections.overview:
The inventory commenced on the surviving knee of the card table, between the tied guards' glares. I laid out the take like a magistrate. One key: iron, plain, sweating faintly with green sap. One ring: gold, heavy, and wrong about the temperature of the room — the band warm as a wrist.

The Guard crossed the room so fast the candle flames leaned.

"I don't trust her," he said. His glove hovered above the gold, not touching. "That's the one. That's the ring I was going to take." Then he did what nobody else had done: he turned the band to the light. Inside the rim, cut very small and very clean, two letters.

"OC."

"This ring is designed to capture souls," he said. "I was taking it to the actual lady. That was the whole—" and he gestured at everything: the vine, the parlor, his severed employment. Bought enough time, and this was what the time had been for.

Nobody spoke. The ring gleamed, smug as a cat. Initials carved into bedframes have a way, in this archive, of turning up again — see [the Oracle](the_oracle) and the [Corvinarus family record](corvinarus_family); the archive apologizes for both.

Hjumpik's eyes moved, slow and geological, to me.

"You called her a fake before anyone said it," the dwarf said. "You were in the ceiling. How did you know?"

"I notice rings," I said, with the dignity of a profession. "It is called observation. Some people read rooms. I audit them."

Not an answer. Filed as: not an answer.

"That doesn't mean we kill everyone," Hjumpik said, looking at the hobgoblin on the hearth.

"They got caught in the crossfire!" I threw both hands up; the right sleeve threatened to re-ignite and was ignored. "I don't like killing. I really don't. But mischief — mischief sometimes goes a little too far. They're still breathing. I think. I don't want to check."

"Arulean." Hjumpik turned to the chair. "What do you think?"

She spat the gag out with her chin, neat as spitting a pit.

"Enough of this."

The air in the room changed hands. I — standing tall at the time — simply folded, knees first, like a puppet struck off its hook; the ring and the key left the table without being carried, jumping flat through the air into her two hands the way nails jump to a magnet. She stood. The ropes lay at her feet like ribbons.

"The soul thing," she said, tasting it on her own tongue, "is true."

*Chain of custody, for the ledger: ring — hers. Ring — mine. Ring — hers again. Elapsed: one hour. I note the inflation rate in dignity per transfer. Receipt pending.*

sections.name: I Am the Plant of the Manor
sections.subtitle: The truest sentence spoken in the house in days
sections.overview:
"Who are you?" Hjumpik said. "Are you really the Lady? We heard things. Guards—" he chose the word with care — "guarding a fake lady."

Her head turned. Below them the house groaned with her.

"Who told you that?" Soft as pruning shears. "I'll make them disappear in an instant."

"I might have heard someone," Hjumpik said.

"Don't worry," I called from the floor. The vines were inspecting me like luggage. "I didn't kill them. They're breathing. I think. Please do not let the plant interrogate me."

"NOT HELPING," Hjumpik said.

The thing with the Lady's face smiled with the Lady's mouth, and then said the truest thing anyone had said in that manor in days.

"This ring." She rolled it between finger and thumb; it purred in the gold light. "Right? She's in here. I am the plant of the manor. The spell that was cast — the plants breach walls, everywhere." She said it the way gardeners discuss weather. "I struck her in the stomach and trapped her in the ring. As she was running."

Toad Lee stepped back into the wainscot vine and did not notice it take his sleeve. The Guard's jaw worked once — fake things; fake people — validated, out loud, by the merchandise.

Hjumpik's hand axe left his hand before the sentence could finish becoming a plan. It buried itself in the tabletop an inch from her finger with a crack that made the candle flames jump.

"Listen." His voice had gravel in it. "All we want — just let my friend go." He blinked once, betrayed by his own stutter. "If you want to take over the manor, I wouldn't like that. But let my friend go."

"Oh, THIS is your friend?" She looked down at me the way one inspects a weed. "He's not very nice. Knocking all these guards out. Ruining my poker game. Stealing from me. Chasing after me."

The cards, curling near the hearth, said nothing in his defense.

"You're not really the Lady." Hjumpik's hands were shaking and the hammer was not. "You lied to him. He acts on the facts."

"Facts," she repeated, charmed. Then she looked at him the way Wario looks at a locked strongbox. "You have something I want."

Four vines went first, unspooling across the floorboards toward Hjumpik's pockets — toward the shape of [Morel's key](morel_feyward_key) against his hip. He stepped back, and the wall behind him was vines now too, leaning in like spectators.

Not good — and then, small, audible, the idea landing behind the dwarf's eyes.

"We're meandering," Toad Lee whispered. "We're just meandering here—"

"Maybe you're right," Hjumpik said, loudly, for the room. "I'll give it to you."

"That's what I like to hear," she said.

A hand unfolded out of the nearest vine — green fingers, too many knuckles, palm up, patient as a collection plate. Hjumpik reached into his pocket. His hand closed on something. It came out.

And a garlic grenade was already in the air.

*WAH! Observe the order of operations. The vine asks for the key. The dwarf reaches for his pocket. The garlic — Toad Lee's, he volunteered it proudly afterward, twice — crosses the room FIRST. The most effective diplomat the Feyward produced all week was a vegetable.*

sections.name: Not Today
sections.subtitle: Fey-bane, fuse, and the descent of the Anvil
sections.overview:
It burst like a kitchen catching fire in reverse: a white-yellow bloom, hot on the eyes. The REEK followed — garlic in its unbottled entirety, the smell of a thousand taverns shouting at once. Every vine in the parlor flinched back like a scalded snake. The Lady’s face went botanical and outraged.

I ran.

My boot caught something. It might have been a lace. It might have been a vine tendril. Destiny remains the leading suspect, but the filing will never settle it. I hit the boards hard enough to bite my tongue. I rolled onto my shoulder.

The vines dropped around me. Green fingers punched into the floorboards and crossed overhead. They closed like the bars of a portcullis. I could see the room through the gaps. I could smell sap, garlic, and my own singed sleeve.

“Not today,” I said. I meant the vines. I meant the Lady. I meant the entire manor, which had become much too confident about catching me.

A Bob-omb came out of the deep personal economy of my person. Its fuse hissed. I set it beside the cage hinge as gently as a man setting down a hat, then scrambled away on all fours.

“WAH! Make room!” I shouted. “I am executing a controlled escape. Do not confuse the crawling with panic!”

The Bob-omb went off in our faces.

Bang is too small a word. Plaster jumped from the ceiling. The last defensible cushion died. Every leaf slapped flat against the walls for one white second. Through the ringing came the sound of a spinning coin: the ring, blown clean off her finger, skipping gold across the boards.

I grabbed it mid-skid and kept going.

Behind me, the smoke parted. The Lady-shape stood inside it with her face hanging wrong. Vines poured from her mouth in curious threads. Her eyes went dark all the way down, ink soaking cloth.

“Keep moving!” I shouted. “Nobody look back unless you enjoy being haunted by vegetables!”

We went out the window.

The descent was architecture, not falling. Hjumpik’s warhammer bit into the ivy-grown mortar — one thunk, one foothold, two. The Anvil of Disaster Inc. climbed down the manor like a man nailing his way home. I followed on my staff, a very tall spider descending an aggrieved pole. My boots skated through mortar dust. Toad Lee rode Hjumpik’s shoulders, wrapped around the dwarf’s neck like cargo with opinions.

Half a floor down, I changed my mind about the ring. I pressed it into Hjumpik’s free palm.

“Here,” I said. “Your pocket. It hates me now. Mine is filing for separation.”

Toad Lee tightened his grip on Hjumpik’s shoulder and announced to the night air, with deep feeling:

“At this point, it’s getting so bad I might HAVE to leave.”

*Garlic: the Vigilance decks. Certain vampire dinner parties. One hag’s kitchen. Now one (1) noblewoman made of hedges. I keep a ledger titled THINGS THAT WORK EVERY TIME. It is a short ledger. At the top of it, in ink, is a bulb. WAH.*

sections.name: The Man at the Window
sections.subtitle: Barrel casualties, a gross deportation, and one sad swordmaster
sections.overview:
The window was warm, and it opened while they hung there like a very damp tapestry.

"Hey," said a young house guard — apron over the breastplate, towel over the elbow, the smell of kitchens behind him. "Hey. You guys okay out there?"

"Mostly," Hjumpik said.

They hung on the wall and traded the news of the world, because that is what walls are for. The tree cutters, the guard said, were doing good work out there. "We're pushing them inwards." The plants, he meant: satyrs with hooked axes herding the overgrowth back toward the middle of the house.

"How's the party?" Toad Lee asked. "The Revel?"

"Well." The guard's face did the thing. "It never ends. But—" He looked down at his towel. "Some people are skeptical. After the whole tree cutters stuff. Uhh — they've been drinking less." He looked kind of sad about it.

"I'm sure the tree destroyed a decent amount of barrels," Hjumpik offered.

"Yeah." The guard brightened and dimmed at once. "And — you didn't hear this — a rogue group of fairies and foes tried to defeat the Revel. It didn't end well for them." He leaned on the sill, dropping his voice the way voices drop around the good parts. "They came charging. Saws and axes. At the Revel. Everyone looked away. It was — gross. By the time I looked back, it was gone. Just — gone." He snapped his fingers, somber as a bellman. "No one else tried to protect the Revel. Well, there was one guy. Ralos? Relis? I just call him Pal." The smile came back crooked. "He's been sad. No one is drinking."

"I need to talk to the heir of the manor," Hjumpik said.

"Why? He's a douche."

"Everyone has a bad side."

"You want me to get him for you?" The guard chewed it. "I thought he was busy—"

"Watch out for upstairs," Toad Lee said quickly. "There's a fake Arulean up there. That is — different. From everything."

"Everything is different," the guard said, philosophically, already turning. "He's on his fifteen-minute mandatory break. I'll get him."

The window stayed open. The party stayed on the wall, hanging in the cool damp air like laundry with opinions.

*A house being eaten from the roots up, and the roster still finds a mandatory fifteen minutes. Say what Waluigi will about the Feyward — and Waluigi will, at length, with slides — the Revel has better labor protections than the Mages' Guild, the Iron Legion, and Wario combined. Waluigi also mourns the barrels, formally. He never even met the barrels.*

sections.name: The Prince's Fifteen Minutes
sections.subtitle: An older sister, a taller order, and the manor's soberest royal
sections.overview:
The heir arrived like bad weather in a dressing gown.

Broken was the word the party used later, kindly; disheveled was the word I used immediately. The orange heir had been through this entire arc — the satyrs, the plan, the drinking, the not-drinking — and it showed in the slope of him, in hair that had stopped attending meetings.

"What was this," he said, without preamble, "about being DIFFERENT?"

"We fought it," I said. "And we won. Also, I would like the record to show that I was nearly eaten by a wall."

Hjumpik thought about the mouthful of vines and the ink-dark eyes, and privately re-filed won under claims requiring review.

"Yeah, I've seen her." The prince's hand sketched at the ceiling. "She was running upstairs. I think she had a private sanctuary she was heading to. We cleared the whole foyer."

"Serves her right," said the room at large, grateful for one bright moment. "It's all clear now."

"You won a battle," Hjumpik said. "Not the war. It's not over."

The prince's gaze came down off the ceiling, and in it was something almost shaped like a man who commanded tree cutters.

"Who are you," Hjumpik said, "to Arulean?"

"She's an older sister." He scratched his head. "She took the throne first. But you knew that."

"...I thought she was a mother," Toad Lee said.

They began arguing — a fey argument, which means two people politely disagreeing about a shrub while I took notes on what the shrub proved about inheritance law. Older sister. Throne first. Mother. Nobody said the word step-anything yet, which mattered later; I wrote it down twice.

"What about the people I knocked out?" I said, when the shrub dispute paused for breath.

"Enough semantics," Hjumpik said.

"What if he takes control of them?" I jabbed one long finger upward, meaning her. "Or she? They are still in that room. All of them."

"I guess—" Hjumpik said, and stopped, because it was the correct question.

Into the silence, I produced from my person a leather pouch and opened it with the ceremony of a master displaying tools: a forged Iron Legion identification card ("Wally," 4th Recon Division, mustache conspicuously absent), a small razor, spirit gum, and a row of noses.

"I can put on a fake mustache," I offered. "Or a nose."

"You're in the same outfit," Hjumpik said. "You're not fooling anyone."

"—Let me finish with the prince." [The kit](waluigi_disguise_kit_wally) vanished, dignity intact, both noses with it. "Mr. Prince. Who is that lady to you?"

"My sister." The prince moved his jaw. "Could be my step-sister. She's a bit old, so — maybe step-sister."

"I won't get into your family business," I said, in my capacity as author of forty volumes of exactly everyone's family business.

"Why are you talking to us now?" Hjumpik said suddenly. "You used to not talk to us."

And the heir did the second surprising thing of the evening, which was to answer.

"When I went downstairs, they put me in charge of the sixth and seventh tree cutter divisions. And I've been — not drinking, recently." His thumb worried the seam of his sleeve. "He has been kinda down lately," he added, about himself, the way very tired men do. "He has been commanding. Ever since they left."

Then he walked past them all and opened the window, letting in the whole cold night — leaves, torch-smoke, and the thin, distant, ridiculous music.

"Let's discuss more," said the prince of the manor. "My tactical map. I'll show you."

*The [balcony plan](feyward_dark_rooms_and_balcony_planning) assumed the prince could be reasoned with. Filed correction: he can also reason BACK, which is rarer and more dangerous — and in this house, at this hour, possibly the first good omen all week. He has a MAP. Nobody in this manor has ever had a map.*

sections.name: Everybody Looks at the Map
sections.subtitle: The window campaign, conducted at height, with minimal grace
sections.overview:
The prince had gone ahead to the war room and thrown its window wide — lamplight on the ledge, the map-table waiting inside like a dinner. Getting there meant going up the outside. I dangled off my staff below the sill, elegant toes skating the mortar, fingers unable to find the stone lip, the whole warm roomful of faces looking down at him.

"My grip," I announced, "is being sabotaged."

"Ready to lift me?" Toad Lee asked, of the air generally.

Hjumpik lifted him. One hand. All the way — Toad Lee rising up the wall like a lantern on a pole, cap first, until his fingers found the sill; the kitchen guard hauled him in by the collar with the deep expertise of a man who has fished many things out of many places.

The nameless guard leaned out next. At the neighboring sill hung the aproned breastplate of his former colleague, and he could not help himself.

"You almost got killed up there," he said. "You ran away. A real guard you are. Real useful."

"Aww," Hjumpik called, sweet as poisoned mead. "How about you SERVE your manor — by picking up Waluigi? Lady's orders."

Lady's orders. The wrong Lady had worn the right one all evening; his face said he knew exactly which Lady was meant — and he squatted over the sill anyway, because a deal is a deal. "Come on then," he growled, bracing one arm out into the dark. "I've got you."

I — already as high up my staff as physics permitted — took the offered wrist, and used it. Swung up on it, planted a boot on the man's pauldron like a rung, swung HIM in through the window ahead — a counterweight with opinions — and vaulted in after, landing tall.

"Don't touch me," I said, with enormous courtesy.

Hjumpik came last: warhammer first, knuckles, boots scraping mortar-dust into the lamplight — caught my offered hand at the top; I actually pulled, which will not be mentioned again — and the Anvil came over the sill and stood up straight in the war room of the heir of the manor.

The map took the whole table.

Pins for the tree cutters: the sixth division inked blocky, the seventh inked apologetic. Barrel tallies run down the margin like a bar bill. The Revel drawn the way weather is drawn — a boundary that keeps moving. The prince planted both hands on the table's edge and began, immediately, in divisions. The kitchen guard hovered. The nameless guard stared at his entire life's work rendered as a pin. Toad Lee leaned on his axe and put his chin on his fist, home at last in the presence of documentation.

For one whole beat, nobody argued.

In Hjumpik's pocket, shifted by the climb, [Morel's key](morel_feyward_key) clicked softly against a ring engraved OC: two small circles of other people's business, riding in the only honest pocket in the house. Faintly, through the floor, from somewhere warm — the fiddle.

> *The Revel never ends.*
> *The Revel never ends.*

The prince kept talking at the map. And because a map is the one thing in that manor nobody had to trust anyone else to believe, they all looked at it.

All of them. At the same thing. At the same time.

*WAH. Filed. Next report begins at the map. Bring rope.*

aftermath:
**Standing.** The false Aurelian — the manor's overgrowth wearing its owner's face and manners — is unmasked and loose, last seen running for a private sanctuary upstairs. The foyer is "cleared," a word currently valued at one card table and zero vines. The real Lady Aurelian is, by her own captor's cheerful account, inside the soul ring: struck mid-flight, in the stomach, as she was running. Her iron key was reclaimed by the plant; the door it opens is unknown.

**Personnel.** The Guard With No Name has defected — name still withheld, following Hjumpik's lead, employment category updated from "furniture" to "gardener at a war." The orange heir commands the 6th and 7th Tree Cutter Divisions from a table-sized tactical map. Ralos Relis — "Pal" — remains the only being who defended the Revel, and its chief mourner. Hobgoblin bodyguards and two house guards: down, tied, breathing (Waluigi declined to verify in writing; the room is now on a plant's side of the wall, which was Waluigi's own question and remains unanswered).

**Materiel.** The [OC soul ring](oc_soul_ring): party custody, in Hjumpik's pocket, beside [Morel's key](morel_feyward_key) and above the wrapped bulk of [Steely's rusted fragments](steely_rusted_fragments), which deserve a burial soon. Expended: one garlic grenade (Toad Lee's, volunteered proudly), one Bob-omb, one card table, two sleeves. Retained: the [Wally kit](waluigi_disguise_kit_wally), the Morning Glory, and an unbroken record of twenty-five feet.

**Exposure.** Every guard in the manor now knows the party's faces. The thing upstairs knows exactly who holds the ring. And a certain pair of initials — carved into bedframes before, carried on soul hardware now — keeps turning up wherever this family hides its doors. See [the Oracle](the_oracle). Waluigi requests, formally, that the initials start turning up somewhere pleasant.
waluigiAssessment:
**1. The mask failed because its manners were too good.** She asked Hjumpik where he was from. The actual Lady of this manor has never asked this party anything. In a fey house, unsolicited curiosity is a seam. Note who caught it instead: a guard who could not say his own name, and an archivist who writes down all jewelry. The party caught nothing. The party never catches anything at the table. Hjumpik confessed his guild's covert status, his life's purpose, and the etymology of his name to vegetation, and Hjumpik is the CAREFUL one.

**2. Names in this house are load-bearing.** A guard who forbids his own name has already resigned; the paperwork simply followed him down the corridor, swords first. That the name he forbade begins like a [defenestrated Shadowfell lord](orangus_cornelius) — and like a robed figure in the [Grafting account](corvinarus_family) — is filed under COINCIDENCES (UNLIKELY), drawer three. Do not say it at the table either.

**3. Chop Bros is not a combat technique; it is trust accounting.** Attempt One failed on load. Attempt Two failed on countdown. Attempt Three — twenty-five feet logged — succeeded the instant they stopped counting. Synchronization is watching, not counting. That said: "I swung out of instinct" is flagged a third time, alongside the missing time, the singing, and [Morel's warning about anchors](feyward_amnesia_vines_morel_steely). The archive does not believe in flukes — not inside this manor, and not twice.

**4. The restraint ledger is improving.** Second hidden room: zero confirmed deaths, against the frozen-room precedent of an [earlier filing](the_feyward_revel_crisis_poison_plants_and_frozen_diplomacy), where at least one person did not thaw. Mischief went slightly less far this time. Growth, logged. Praised, reluctantly. The garlic grenade and the Bob-omb demonstrate that Waluigi's doctrine of escalation now includes an off-ramp, provided the off-ramp explodes.

**5. The OC ring is now the most important object in the branch.** Oracle initials — previously carved into bedframes by whoever built this family's accursed plumbing — now appear on soul-capture hardware carried by vegetation impersonating nobility. Either the Oracle has a manufacturer, or had one. Hjumpik's pocket currently holds Morel's key and the ring: the dwarf is becoming the manor's escrow agent. It is the only safe arrangement in the branch, and Waluigi hates that it is the only safe arrangement.

**RECOMMENDATION:** Interview the ring's occupant through a professional (ghost-adjacent staff are available and bored). Do not smash it. Do not sell it. Do not let Wario appraise, hold, polish, or "just look at" it. Do not, under any circumstances, including formal occasions, wear it. Find the sanctuary upstairs before she finishes unpacking — a plant that has had weeks with a private room has had a private room for weeks. The map is the first honest object this house has produced. The next filing begins there. WAH.
